title: Founder case: Dropbox shows a demo first

sources.claim: Before the product was ready for the public, Drew Houston posted a short demo video of Dropbox with a sign-up form for a beta waiting list, and the waiting list grew sharply after the video was shared online.

sections.skill: Apply a documented test: a demo with a sign-up list

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Houston share before the product was public?

choices.text: A finished product sold in stores

questions.correct_answer: A short demo video
questions.intro: Documented history: before Dropbox was ready for the public, cofounder Drew Houston posted a short demo video showing how the file-syncing product would work, with a way to join a waiting list for the beta (early test) version. After the video was shared online, the waiting list grew sharply. Accounts differ on the exact numbers, so none are used here. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation): a clear demonstration can test interest before a product is finished, but sign-ups are interest, not payment. One success story does not guarantee the same result.
questions.feedback: He shared a demo video with a waiting-list sign-up.

questions.prompt: A waiting-list sign-up measures what?
questions.correct_answer: Interest
questions.intro: A sign-up list measures interest: people giving their email to hear more. A payment measures commitment: people giving money. Both are useful, but they are different. Many people sign up for things they never buy. If a waiting list is large, the next step is to check how many will pay, for example with a paid early-access offer.
questions.feedback: Giving an email shows interest.

questions.prompt: Which measures commitment?
questions.correct_answer: Paying for early access
